prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the cleanest recent case in the shortlist of a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, which located the magic angle and the flat bands) followed by an unambiguous experimental discovery in nature (Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity). That pairing of idea and observation is what I look for. The discovery created a genuinely new, tunable platform for strongly correlated matter, has been reproduced by many independent groups across several moire systems, and the credited trio is compact and coherent. It also has the broadest opening support in this run: top-three on four ballots, eight rankings, and the highest Borda total of any shortlisted candidate. I held my first place after reading colleagues, because the cross-field consensus on it is wider than for any rival, even if few members ranked it first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity and the nature of the correlated insulators are still debated, so a citation must be worded around the observed states and the flat-band prediction rather than a settled mechanism. The experimental credit is also narrower than the history: Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers, and other experimental groups, are outside the credited names, and earlier moire-band theory by other authors could be raised. Reproducibility and twist-angle inhomogeneity remain practical issues. If the committee thinks the field is still moving too fast, topological insulators (B016) or the optical lattice clock (B059) are the better-settled alternatives.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators (B016) first on the strength of Kane-Mele Z2 theory plus the HgTe observation by Molenkamp, and places twisted bilayer graphene second, urging that its rationale be limited to what is established because the pairing mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with the caution on the superconducting mechanism and would word the citation around the predicted flat bands and the observed correlated and superconducting states, as above. Where I differ is on priority. B016 is certainly a strong discovery and I rank it second myself, but it carries a persistent attribution problem (Mele, Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the late Shoucheng Zhang) and sits close to the 2016 prize on topological phases. Magic-angle graphene has a cleaner theory-plus-experiment structure and is not covered by an earlier prize. I would not call B016 overdue so much as awkward to credit, and I would take it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B059) first: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record accuracy made optical frequency metrology the leading precision tool, with uncertainties near 1e-18, and a two-person prize is clean.
responses.response: The two-person credit is clean and the achievement is real; I ranked it fourth, not low. My hesitation is that much of the reach (redefinition of the second, geodesy, tests of constants) is still prospective, and the committee will need to separate this from the 2005 comb prize and from ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups such as NIST and SYRTE. I do not think those are fatal, and your point that the metrology payoff is already demonstrated at the 1e-18 level is fair. I would not oppose B059 as the prize, and keep it as my second alternative, but I do not think it is more decisive than a discovery that opened a new correlated-matter platform.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory (B046) first as the controlled account of the Mott transition and of correlated electrons, but places twisted bilayer graphene fourth, citing the unsettled superconducting mechanism and the uncredited experimental co-discoverers.
responses.response: Your point that the experimental credit is incomplete is correct and I return to it under uncertainties. I would still separate a settled mechanism from a settled discovery: the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle is robust and reproduced, while the mechanism is open, and the Nobel Prize has often honoured discoveries before their mechanism was understood. DMFT is a major theoretical method, but its weight is in a computational framework whose predictive power for specific materials you yourself flag as debated, and only you ranked it, so I would want to hear what others think before treating it as a leading prize candidate.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube astrophysical neutrinos (B043) first as the opening of a new observational window, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as a workable credit.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube third in my own opening ballot and value the observational character of the discovery, which fits my preference for findings made in nature. The astrophysical interpretation is still developing, since most of the diffuse flux has no identified source, and attribution across a very large collaboration is hard. That combination makes me place it behind the graphene case, but it stays a serious candidate and is the best option if the committee wants an astroparticle prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-person credit that leaves out Yuan Cao and other first-author experimentalists of the 2018 papers, or would prefer to credit the experiment more widely.
Whether the field is judged mature enough while the superconducting pairing mechanism remains disputed, and how a citation can be worded to avoid committing to it.
Whether B016 or B059 would be easier to defend on attribution grounds than B034, and how the 2016 and 2025 prizes should weigh in.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group) are in string theory and gravitation and have no evident link to the credited names on this shortlist. Twisted bilayer graphene is also outside my own research field.
